'''James Andrew Jones''' (born October 4, 1980) is an American professional [[basketball]] executive and former player. He is the executive vice president, head of basketball operations for the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). Jones played 14 seasons in the NBA from 2003 to 2017. He was also the general manager and president of basketball operations for the [[Phoenix Suns]].

Jones was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] at [[American High School (Miami-Dade County, Florida)|American High School]] in [[Hialeah, Florida]]. He averaged 25 points per game as a senior, earning Class 6A Player of the Year and First-team All-State honors. He then played [[college basketball]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes men's basketball|Miami Hurricanes]] of the [[University of Miami]], where he was a three-year starter and finished his career averaging 11 points per game. Jones was named Third-team All-[[Big East Conference|Big East]] his junior year and Second-team [[Verizon]] Academic [[All-American]] his senior year. He was inducted into the University of Miami Sports Hall of Fame in 2014.

Jones was drafted by the [[Indiana Pacers]] in the second round of the [[2003 NBA draft]]. He went on to play for the Pacers, Phoenix Suns, [[Portland Trail Blazers]], [[Miami Heat]] and [[Cleveland Cavaliers]]. He won three NBA championships, two with the Heat and one with the Cavaliers. He and teammate [[LeBron James]] reached the [[NBA Finals]] for seven consecutive years from 2011 to 2017. Jones was never on an NBA team with a losing record and only missed the playoffs once—with the Trail Blazers in 2007–08. He finished third in the NBA in three-point percentage during the 2007–08 season and won the [[Three-Point Contest]] in 2011. His nickname is "Champ".

In July 2017, Jones was named the director of player personnel for the Suns. He was promoted to general manager in April 2019. After the Suns reached the playoffs for the first time since 2010, Jones was named the 2020–21 [[NBA Executive of the Year]]. He was later promoted to president of basketball operations and general manager after the team won a franchise-record 64 regular season games during the 2021–22 season.

==Early life==
Jones was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in basketball at [[American High School (Miami-Dade County, Florida)|American High School]] in [[Hialeah, Florida]]. He averaged 25.2 points, 12 rebounds, 2.5 assists, two steals, and six blocks per game his senior season, earning First-team All-State and First-team All-Dade honors.<ref name="miami"/> He was also named the Class 6A Player of the Year and the [[Miami Herald]] Boys' Basketball Player of the Year. Jones was the team MVP his junior and senior years and once blocked 16 shots in one game.<ref name="miami">{{cite web | url=http://www.hurricanesports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=28700&ATCLID=205555758 | title=James Jones | website=HurricaneSports.com |publisher=[[University of Miami]] | access-date=June 21, 2016 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160622002230/http://www.hurricanesports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=28700&ATCLID=205555758 | archive-date=June 22, 2016 }}</ref>

==College career==
Jones played [[college basketball]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes men's basketball|Miami Hurricanes]] of the [[University of Miami]] from 1999 to 2003.<ref name="miami"/> During his time at Miami, he majored in finance, was a member of the [[National Honor Society]], and had a 3.41 grade point average.<ref name="miami"/><ref name="nba"/> He played in 33 games, averaging 3.9 points and 1.9 rebounds per game, during his freshman year in 1999. He started all 29 games for the Hurricanes his sophomore year, averaging 11.9 points, 5.9 rebounds, 1.2 assists, 1.2 steals and 1.6 blocks per game. Jones shot a team-best 41-of-87 on three-pointers for a .471 percentage.<ref name="miami"/> He started all 31 games for the team his junior season, averaging 12.8 points, 6.3 rebounds, 1.5 assists, 2.4 blocks and 1.3 steals, garnering Third-team All-[[Big East Conference|Big East]] and 2002 [[Verizon]] Academic All-District III accolades.<ref name="miami"/> He started all 28 games his senior year, averaging 16.9 points, 6.0 rebounds, 1.8 assists, 1.6 steals and 1.8 blocks, earning Honorable Mention All-Big East and Second-team Verizon Academic All-American recognition. Jones led the team in blocks and rebounds as a senior.<ref name="miami"/>
 
He played in 122 games, starting 89, during college and finished his career averaging 11.1 points, 5.0 rebounds, 1.2 assists, 1.1 steals and 1.6 blocks per game.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/players/james-jones-1.html | title=James Jones | publisher=[[Sports Reference LLC]] | work=sports-reference.com | access-date=February 10, 2017}}</ref><ref name="miami"/> He started 89 consecutive games from the 2000–01 season to the 2002–03 season. Jones also earned Big East All-Academic honors all four seasons and was the Hurricanes' first Verizon Academic All-American selection.<ref name="miami"/> He was inducted into the University of Miami Sports Hall of Fame in 2014.<ref name="Navarro">{{Cite web |url=http://www.miamiherald.com/sports/college/acc/university-of-miami/article1962585.html |title=Miami natives James Jones, Andre Johnson set to join UM Sports Hall of Fame |last1=Degnan |first1=Susan Miller |last2=Navarro |first2=Manny |date=April 10, 2014 |work=[[Miami Herald]] |access-date=June 21, 2016}}</ref>

===Phoenix Suns (2005–2007)===
Jones was traded by the Pacers to the [[Phoenix Suns]] on August 25, 2005, in exchange for a [[Mike Taylor (basketball player)|2008 second-round draft pick]].<ref name="pacers"/> He played in 75 games, starting 24, for the Suns during the [[2005–06 NBA season|2005–06 season]], averaging 9.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 23.6 minutes per game. He missed seven games due to a variety of injuries.<ref name="nba"/> Jones's turnover percentage of 5.23 turnovers committed per 100 plays during the 2005–06 season set an NBA record for lowest single-season turnover percentage. It was fourth place on the all-time list as of the end of the [[2015–16 NBA season|2015–16 season]].<ref name="trn">{{cite web|url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/tov_pct_season.html |title=NBA & ABA Single Season Leaders and Records for Turnover Pct |work=Basketball Reference|publisher=[[Sports Reference, LLC]] |access-date=June 26, 2016 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160626225028/http://www.basketball-reference.com/leaders/tov_pct_season.html |archive-date=June 26, 2016 }}</ref> The NBA did not start recording individual turnovers until the [[1977–78 NBA season|1977–78 season]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Grasso, John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nZUarsZyzokC&q=The+National+Basketball+Association+did+not+record+turnover+statistics+until+the+1977%E2%80%9378+season&pg=PA358 |title=Historical Dictionary of Basketball |publisher=[[Scarecrow Press]] |year=2010 |pages=358|isbn = 9780810875067}}</ref>

He appeared in 76 games, with 7 starts, for the team during the [[2006–07 NBA season|2006–07 season]], averaging 6.4 points, 2.3 rebounds and 18.1 minutes a game. He was a DNP-CD six times. Jones made 45 consecutive free throws from January 5 to March 29, the longest consecutive free throws made streak in the NBA during the 2006–07 season.<ref name="nba"/>

He missed one game due to an intestinal virus and was a DNP-CD 35 times. Jones was also healthy but on the inactive list ten games.<ref name="nba"/>

==Executive career==
On July 19, 2017, Jones was named the director of player personnel for the [[Phoenix Suns]], effectively ending his 14-year NBA career.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nba.com/suns/suns-extend-ryan-mcdonough-general-manager-name-james-jones-vice-president-basketball-operations | title=Suns Extend Ryan McDonough as General Manager, Name James Jones alongside assistant general manager Trevor Bukstein after the previous general manager, [[Ryan McDonough (NBA executive)|Ryan McDonough]], was fired.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nba.com/suns/press-release/suns-relieve-ryan-mcdonough-general-manager-duties | title=Suns Relieve Ryan McDonough of General Manager Duties | publisher=[[NBA.com]] | date=October 8, 2018 | access-date=October 8, 2018}}</ref> During the 2018–19 season, he worked with Bukstein on two trades for the Suns: trading [[Trevor Ariza]] for [[Kelly Oubre Jr.]] and [[Austin Rivers]] in December 2018 and [[Ryan Anderson (basketball, born 1988)|Ryan Anderson]] for [[Tyler Johnson (basketball)|Tyler Johnson]] and [[Wayne Ellington]] in February 2019.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://basketball.realgm.com/nba/teams/Phoenix-Suns/23/Transaction_History/2019 | title=2018-2019 Phoenix Suns Transaction History | publisher=basketball.realgm.com | accessdate=13 September 2024}}</ref> On April 11, 2019, the Suns removed the interim tag from Jones' title, naming him the team's general manager, with Bukstein remaining as assistant general manager.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nba.com/suns/suns-name-james-jones-general-manager-0 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190411163436/https://www.nba.com/suns/suns-name-james-jones-general-manager-0 | url-status=dead | archive-date=2019-04-11 | title=Suns Name James Jones General Manager | publisher=[[NBA.com]] | date=April 11, 2019 | accessdate=13 September 2024}}</ref>

During the 2019 off-season, Jones orchestrated changes that appeared questionable on the surface, such as firing head coach [[Igor Kokoškov]] after only one season (albeit hiring [[Monty Williams]] soon afterward),<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/sports/nba/suns/2019/04/24/phoenix-suns-jones-made-decision-fire-kokoskov-after-one-season/3559391002/ | title=James Jones seeks new beginning for Phoenix Suns after firing Igor Kokoskov | work=[[The Arizona Republic]] | date=April 24, 2019 | accessdate=13 September 2024 | author=Rankin, Duane}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wojnarowski |first=Adrian  |author-link=Adrian Wojnarowski |date=April 22, 2019 |title=Suns fire Kokoskov; Williams eyed, sources say |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/26583507/suns-fire-kokoskov-williams-eyed-sources-say |access-date=December 8, 2020 |publisher=[[ESPN]]}}</ref> executing multiple trades in the [[2019 NBA draft]], including [[T. J. Warren]] to the [[Indiana Pacers]] for cash considerations, trading down from the 6th pick to pick up both [[Dario Šarić]] and the 11th draft pick ([[Cameron Johnson]]) from the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]], and trading a late 2020 first-round pick to the [[Boston Celtics]] for [[Aron Baynes]] and the 24th pick ([[Ty Jerome]]),<ref>{{cite web | url=https://hoopshabit.com/2019/07/03/phoenix-suns-plan-place-asset-management-poor/ | title=Phoenix Suns: Plan is in place, but asset management is poor | publisher=HoopsHabit.com | date=Jul 3, 2019 | accessdate=13 September 2024 | author=Bourguet, Gerald}}</ref> and even picking up [[Ricky Rubio]] in free agency via trading multiple picks and players with the [[Memphis Grizzlies]] to free up more salary.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://arizonasports.com/story/1996295/nba-free-agency-grades-mixed-reactions-on-suns-ricky-rubio-signing/ | title=NBA free agency grades: Mixed reactions on Suns' Ricky Rubio signing | publisher=ArizonaSports.com | date=July 1, 2020 | access-date=December 8, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cbssports.com/nba/news/2019-nba-offseason-roster-changes-grades-player-movement-signings-trades-for-every-team/ | title=2019 NBA offseason roster changes: Grades, player movement, signings, trades for every team | publisher=[[CBS Sports]] | date=July 25, 2019 | access-date=December 8, 2020}}</ref> Despite the mixed reception, Jones' moves would help the Suns achieve their best record in five seasons, before the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] hit U.S. shores in 2020, with a 26–39 record before the season [[Suspension of the 2019–20 NBA season|was suspended]]. When the season resumed in the [[2020 NBA Bubble]], the Suns managed to finish with an 8–0 run in Orlando, with their only significant roster change adding [[NBA G League|G League]] guard [[Cameron Payne]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://clutchpoints.com/suns-everything-you-need-to-know-about-the-historic-bubble-team/|title=Everything you need to know about the historic bubble Phoenix Suns|publisher=ClutchPoints|last=Honaker|first=Kenny|date=August 13, 2021|access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/teams/PHO/ | title=Phoenix Suns | work=Basketball Reference |publisher=[[Sports Reference LLC]] | accessdate=13 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/teams/PHO/2020.html | title=2019-20 Phoenix Suns Roster and Stats | work=Basketball Reference |publisher=[[Sports Reference LLC]]| accessdate=13 September 2024}}</ref>

With the surprising improvement in the bubble, Jones orchestrated another major trade in November 2020, this time trading Kelly Oubre Jr., Ricky Rubio, Ty Jerome, [[Jalen Lecque]], and a protected 2022 first-round pick to the [[Oklahoma City Thunder]] for [[Abdel Nader]] and All-Star point guard [[Chris Paul]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nba.com/suns/features/suns-complete-trade-chris-paul-abdel-nader | title=Suns Complete Trade For Chris Paul & Abdel Nader | publisher=[[NBA.com]] | date=November 16, 2020 | access-date=December 8, 2020}}</ref> Jones looked to bolster team depth in the delayed [[2020 NBA draft]] period by selecting [[Jalen Smith]] at pick 10 and picking up [[Jae Crowder]], [[E'Twaun Moore]], [[Langston Galloway]], and [[Damian Jones (basketball)|Damian Jones]] in the shortened 2020 free agency period in the hopes of ending their decade-long playoff drought.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/sports/nba/suns/2020/11/25/phoenix-suns-among-biggest-winners-nba-free-agency-nba-offseason/6428740002/|title=Phoenix Suns a threat in Western Conference after moves in NBA free agency, offseason|work=[[The Arizona Republic]]|last=Cluff|first=Jeremy|date=November 25, 2020|access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brightsideofthesun.com/2020/11/23/21590456/center-of-the-sun-phoenix-suns-remade-roster-looks-to-be-the-strongest-since-2009-10-nba|publisher=[[SB Nation]]|title=Center of the Sun: Remade Suns roster looks to be the strongest since 2009–10|last=Argent|first=Ron|date=November 23, 2020|access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref> The Suns later made the [[2021 NBA playoffs]]; the team's first postseason appearance since 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.ph/nba/story/_/id/31495149/phoenix-suns-james-jones-close-ties-lebron-james-braces-lakers-series|title=Phoenix Suns' James Jones, with close ties to LeBron James, braces for Lakers series|publisher=[[ESPN]]|last=McMenamin|first=Dave|date=May 23, 2021|access-date=June 18, 2021}}</ref> Because of the Suns' dramatic improvement, Jones earned the 2020–21 [[NBA Executive of the Year Award]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Phoenix's James Jones wins 2020–21 NBA Basketball Executive of the Year award|url=https://www.nba.com/news/phoenix-suns-james-jones-2021-executive-year|publisher=[[NBA.com]]|access-date=June 20, 2021|date=June 20, 2021}}</ref> The Suns reached the [[2021 NBA Finals]], but lost the series in six games to the [[Milwaukee Bucks]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2021 NBA Finals: Suns vs. Bucks |url=https://www.nba.com/playoffs/2021/the-finals |access-date=2024-02-19 |publisher=[[NBA.com]]}}</ref>

The Suns won a franchise-record 64 regular season games during the 2021–22 season. Jones was promoted from general manager to president of basketball operations and general manager on November 28, 2022.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nba.com/suns/news/suns-promote-james-jones-to-president-of-basketball-operations-and-general-manager | title=SUNS PROMOTE JAMES JONES TO PRESIDENT OF BASKETBALL OPERATIONS AND GENERAL MANAGER | publisher=[[NBA.com]] | date=November 28, 2022 | accessdate=13 September 2024}}</ref> The Suns finished with a 36–46 record in 2024–25, their first losing season since 2019–20.<ref name="advisor">{{cite news | url=https://www.azcentral.com/story/sports/nba/suns/2025/05/01/phoenix-suns-elevate-vp-brian-gregory-to-gm-shift-james-jones-to-senior-advisor/83393470007/ | title=Phoenix Suns elevate VP Brian Gregory to general manager, shift James Jones to senior advisor | work=[[The Arizona Republic]] | date=1 May 2025 | accessdate=1 May 2025 | author=Rankin, Duane}}</ref> Afterwards [[Brian Gregory]] was named the team's new general manager and Jones was demoted to senior advisor.<ref name="advisor"/><ref>{{cite web|title=PHOENIX SUNS ANNOUNCE BASKETBALL OPERATIONS CHANGES|url=https://www.nba.com/suns/news/phoenix-suns-announce-basketball-operations-changes|publisher=[[NBA.com]]|access-date=May 1, 2025|date=May 1, 2025}}</ref> On July 9, 2025, Jones left the Suns to become the NBA's executive vice president, head of basketball operations.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nba/2025/07/09/nba-james-jones-joe-dumars-replacement/84522510007/ | title=NBA names James Jones executive vice president, replacing Joe Dumars | work=[[USA Today]] | date=July 9, 2025 | accessdate=9 July 2025 | author=Axson, Scooby}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Jones is a [[Christianity|Christian]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Duduit |first1=Del |title=James Jones of The Cavaliers Lives by Deep-Rooted Faith |date=May 2, 2017 |url=https://centralfloridavoice.com/james-jones-of-the-cavaliers-lives-by-deep-rooted-faith/ |publisher=CentralFloridaVoice.com |access-date=31 October 2021 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He and his wife Destiny have a son named James Dylan Jones and two daughters named Jadynn Alyssa Jones and Jodie Marissa Jones.<ref name="nba"/> Jones's nicknames include "Champ", "J. J." and "JHoops" (pronounced Joops).<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nba.com/cavaliers/news/features/playerfile-jones-140817 | title=Season Wrap-Up: JAMES JONES | publisher=[[NBA.com]] | date=August 17, 2015 | access-date=June 21, 2016 | author=Gabriele, Joe}}</ref><ref name="nba"/><ref name="espn"/> The James Jones Legacy Foundation was founded in 2009.<ref name="nba"/> He is also a managing partner of the consulting firm Jones and Jones Strategic Consulting.<ref name="jones">{{cite web|url=http://jamesjones22.com/my-story |title=My Story |publisher=JamesJones22.com |access-date=January 10, 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110185020/http://jamesjones22.com/my-story |archive-date=January 10, 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.corporationsearchus.com/Florida/JONES-JONES-STRATEGIC-CONSULTING-LLC |title=JONES & JONES STRATEGIC CONSULTING, LLC |publisher=CorporationSearchUS.com |access-date=January 10, 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110193238/http://www.corporationsearchus.com/Florida/JONES-JONES-STRATEGIC-CONSULTING-LLC |archive-date=January 10, 2017 }}</ref> Jones previously owned an [[urban redevelopment]] company called James Jones Ventures.<ref name="nba"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://corporationsearchus.com/Florida/JAMES-JONES-VENTURES-LLC |title=JAMES JONES VENTURES, LLC |publisher=CorporationSearchUS.com |access-date=January 10, 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110193206/http://corporationsearchus.com/Florida/JAMES-JONES-VENTURES-LLC |archive-date=January 10, 2017 }}</ref> He began hosting an annual basketball camp called JHoops Live in 2009.<ref name="nba"/> He also runs a camp called Crew 22 Training Camp.<ref name="jones"/> Jones appeared on the television show ''[[Kitchen Nightmares]]'' in 2010.<ref name="nba"/>

Jones's uncle, [[Ricky Gutiérrez]], played in [[Major League Baseball]].<ref name="miami"/> Jones's aunt, Lisa Jones played basketball at the University of Miami from 1988 to 1990.<ref name="miami"/> His cousin Mionsha Gay also played at the University of Miami.<ref name="nba"/> His aunt, Hope Jones, and his cousin, Shelnita Jackson, played basketball at [[Barry University]].<ref name="nba"/> Jones's father Jay Lee played at [[Southern University]] while his uncle Mitchell Lee played at the [[University of Minnesota]] and his cousin Shawn Brailsford played at [[Marshall University]].<ref name="nba"/>

Jones was previously the secretary-treasurer of the [[National Basketball Players Association|NBA Players Association]] (NBPA).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nbpa.com/leadership/ |title=Leadership |publisher=[[National Basketball Players Association]] |access-date=July 19, 2017 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170206032138/http://nbpa.com/leadership/ |archive-date=February 6, 2017 }}</ref>
